content:
Whether you're typing in all caps, editing an email draft, or using that "shift" key on your keyboard, you probably toss around the words "uppercase" and "lowercase" every day without thinking twice.

But have you ever wondered where these terms come from? Why are they called "cases," and why are they divided into "upper" and "lower"? HuffPost enlisted linguistic experts to break it all down.

"These terms are actually more literal than people might realize," Noel Wolf, a culture and language expert at the language-learning platform Babbel, told HuffPost. "The words come from the printing press, where typesetters would store individual metal letters in wooden trays (called cases). Capital letters went in a case positioned higher up, while the more frequently used smaller letters sat below, in a more easily accessible case. So the names are actually describing where the printer reached to grab a letter, not the height of the letters on the page."

To understand the origin of these words, we need to rewind several centuries to the era of movable type, when printing professionals were called compositors. The first documented use of "uppercase" and "lowercase" appears in Joseph Moxon's 1683 printing manual, "Mechanick Exercises: Or, the Doctrine of Handy-Works Applied to the Art of Printing."

Madeline Enos, a language trends expert at the language-learning platform Preply, pointed out: "Moxon, in describing the compositor's equipment, references 'Upper-Case' and 'Lower-Case.'" These terms eventually moved beyond the printing world and became the everyday words we all use to refer to capital and small letters.

English, therefore, retains a fragment of printing history in its everyday vocabulary.

"It's an industry term that made its way from the workshop into everyday standard usage, and I think most people don't know what 'uppercase' and 'lowercase' originally referred to," Enos said.

She said: "The printing press came to England in 1476, initially in very few locations. But by the end of the century, there were quite a few printers, and during this time, the jargon of printing was constantly being added to—although not many people were working together, they would often invent specific terms for [their tools]."

But how do we know what terms those printers invented?

Adams said: "We have to rely on manuscripts and printed materials as evidence. The printing industry was just getting started, but it was still very limited, and printers didn't think there was much money in printing books about printing—so terms like 'uppercase' and 'lowercase' took a while to be recorded. The earliest evidence of printers sorting letters into cases dates to 1553, but no one mentions 'uppercase' and 'lowercase' until Joseph Moxon's 'Mechanick Exercises' was published."

As mentioned, this important early printing work, published in 1683, describes in detail the traditional layout of the type cases in printing presses.

Adams said: "We now think of 'lowercase' and 'uppercase' as one word, but originally they were 'lower case' and 'upper case,' reflecting that there were actual physical cases or boxes used to sort type. By convention, so-called capital letters were placed in the upper case, and small letters in the lower case. That, in a nutshell, is the answer!"

But this system of writing actually predates printing by far.

Enos pointed out: "Capital and small letters existed long before the terms 'uppercase' and 'lowercase' came about." Capital letters are the older of the two—they originated in Roman monumental inscriptions, like the ones we see on the Pantheon or Trajan's Column.

Small letters, also called minuscules, came later, evolving with handwriting.

Enos said: "As scribes wrote faster, letter forms became rounder and easier to produce, and developed features like ascenders and descenders—parts of letters that extend beyond the main body, like the upward stroke in 'b' or the downward stroke in 'p.'"

This dual system of capital and small letters was formally established in the late 8th century by Charlemagne.

Enos said: "To standardize the Latin texts across his empire, he commissioned scholars to develop a clear script for copying manuscripts—now known as Carolingian minuscule. Scribes of the time combined the everyday small letters with the older Roman capitals for headings and emphasis, essentially creating the two-tier system still in use today. Printers centuries later simply took this pre-existing convention and incorporated it into physical cases and boxes."

Not every language uses capital letters.

Interestingly, for English speakers, this capital/small letter system is not the global norm.

Enos said: "It's worth noting that the majority of the world's writing systems are unicase. Arabic, Hebrew, Korean (Hangul), Thai, Devanagari, Georgian, and Chinese characters are all represented in a single form. Bicameral scripts include Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Armenian, and a few others."

In practice, these writing systems handle things like sentence beginnings and proper nouns in different ways.

Wolf said: "They use spacing, punctuation, and context to achieve what capitalization does in English."

Even among languages that use the same bicameral system, capitalization conventions differ.

Adams said: "Historically, across Europe, capitals or capital letters were used at the beginning of sentences and for proper nouns, but it wasn't a hard-and-fast rule—different scribes did things differently. By the 18th century, there were already many different styles of capitalization, and usage varied across European languages. German capitalizes all nouns and formal pronouns. French only capitalizes proper nouns, and nationalities when referring to people as nouns, but not when they're used as adjectives."

For language learners, this can present a real challenge.

Enos said: "'Case' is something native English speakers take for granted, but for language learners accustomed to a unicase writing system, it can be a new concept. People used to reading Arabic, Korean, or Chinese have to learn new vocabulary, and they also have to learn a new case system, where the same letter can look quite different—A and a—and capitals have their own rules. Learning a new language is often as much about learning to see things differently as it is about learning to speak differently."

The words "uppercase" and "lowercase" aren't common across bicameral languages, either.

Enos said: "French uses majuscule and minuscule, derived directly from the Latin maiusculus—meaning 'somewhat greater'—and minusculus—'somewhat lesser.' German uses Großbuchstabe and Kleinbuchstabe, literally 'big letter' and 'small letter.'"

Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese terms all derive from the same Latin roots "maius" and "minus": "mayúsculas and minúsculas," "maiuscolo and minuscolo," and "maiúsculas and minúsculas," respectively.

Wolf said: "Other languages have adopted more direct, size-based descriptions. Dutch uses 'hoofdletters,' literally 'head letters,' for capitals, and 'kleine letters' for small letters. Turkish uses 'büyük harf,' meaning 'big letter,' and 'küçük harf,' meaning 'small letter.' Swedish uses 'versaler' and 'gemener.' Norwegian and Danish both use 'store' and 'små bokstaver' or 'små bogstaver'—that is, 'big letters' and 'small letters.' Russian distinguishes between 'заглавная буква,' meaning 'title' or 'beginning' letter, and 'строчная буква,' meaning 'body line' letter."

Adams noted that French also has a parallel construction, "bas de casse," for lowercase—literally "bottom of the case"—and "haut de casse," or "top of the case," for uppercase. However, these usages are relatively rare.

It's worth noting that not all languages with capital and small letters use them in the same way.

Wolf said: "German is a great example. Unlike English, it capitalizes every noun, not just sentence beginnings and proper nouns—a convention that became standardized in the 18th century. So even among languages that share the same bicameral system, there are different ideas about what capitalization is for."

These various features and origins are precisely what makes comparing languages so enlightening.

Wolf said: "It's a reminder that a lot of what seems like grammar is really unupdated industrial history. Every time we talk about capital letters, we're still describing wooden type cases that fell out of use centuries ago. Comparing different languages tends to bring these things to the surface—when you see another language solve the same naming problem differently, you start to notice these 'fossils.'"
